name: Chewing for jaw

lead: Chewing for jaw, often called jawmaxxing, means chewing tough gum such as mastic or hard foods for long periods to enlarge the masseter muscles and strengthen the jaw. It is popular in looksmaxxing forums as a way to look more defined at the lower face.
Masseter enlargement from heavy chewing is recognised in medical literature. Claims that chewing reshapes the jaw bone or improves the profile have not been studied in published trials.

paras: The masseter is a main chewing muscle at the angle of the jaw, and like other skeletal muscle it can enlarge with sustained use. Proponents add the idea that bone adapts to muscle loading as well. No study tests whether chewing regimens change facial bone in people.

Medical sources note that constant gum chewing or clenching can enlarge the masseter and has been linked to temporomandibular problems. A study of 323 adolescent girls examined gum chewing, jaw play and temporomandibular symptoms. A forum user reports worn molars and a face that looked bloated after years of mewing and mastic gum chewing.

lead: Chewing for jaw, also called jawmaxxing, is a practice in looksmaxxing communities in which people chew hard gum, particularly mastic gum, or tough foods to develop the jaw muscles and, according to proponents, the jaw's appearance [1][2]. It is often paired with mewing, chin tucks and neck exercises [2].

The masseter muscle can enlarge in people who clench or grind their teeth or chew gum constantly, and the enlargement may make the face look asymmetrical or wider [3]. Whether chewing changes the underlying bone, or improves jawline definition, has not been tested in published studies.
infobox: Mastic gum, other tough gum, hard foods

paras: Practitioners chew tough gum or food for extended periods, often alongside other regimens. One forum routine lists daily mastic gum chewing in a chin-tucked position, mouth taping at night, hard mewing, neck stretching and training, and nose breathing [2]. Another thread presents a 'guide' to jawmaxxing built around tongue posture and facial forces over time [1].

The masseter is thick and strong, supplied by the mandibular branch of the trigeminal nerve, and closes the jaw [3]. Enlargement from bruxism or constant gum chewing is usually bilateral and typically painless, and can mimic other conditions; patients often seek care for its appearance [3]. A review of mastication notes that features such as the number of teeth, bite force and salivary flow influence how a person chews [4].
No studies found. No published trial has tested chewing regimens for facial or jaw appearance.

Related research addresses other questions. A questionnaire study of 323 girls aged 15 to 16 found gum chewing was very common (62.4%), with a mean of 3.95 hours per day among those who chewed, and examined its association with temporomandibular disorder symptoms [5]. Another report examined gum chewing and jaw muscle fatigue and pain [6]. A systematic review studied the effect of malocclusion on jaw motor function and chewing in children [7].

A forum user who said he had mewed and chewed mastic gum for years reported that his dentist described his molars as worn like those of an elderly person, and that his masseter hypertrophy made his face look bloated because of limited cheekbone width [8]. Medical sources link enlargement of the masseter to constant gum chewing and possible temporomandibular joint problems [3].

lore.intro: Chewing is promoted on looksmax.org as the one 'bonehack' with a plausible muscular effect, though members debate whether the result is desirable [1][8].
